y' =My+2e^{3t}\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad 
M=\begin{pmatrix}\alpha&\beta\\ \gamma&\alpha\end{pmatrix},
\quad y(0)=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-2\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Because  

\[
M=\alpha I+N,\qquad 
N=\begin{pmatrix}0&\beta\\ \gamma&0\end{pmatrix},
\qquad 
N^{2}= \beta\gamma\,I,
\]

let  

\[
\omega=\sqrt{\beta\gamma},\qquad 
\Delta=(3-\alpha)^{2}-\beta\gamma .
\]

The matrix exponential is  

\[
e^{Mt}=e^{\alpha t}\Bigl(\cosh(\omega t)\,I+
\frac{\sinh(\omega t)}{\omega}\,N\Bigr).
\]

A particular solution of the form \(y_{p}=Ae^{3t}\) is obtained from  

\[
(3I-M)A=2\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}
\Longrightarrow 
A=2(3I-M)^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}
 =\frac{2}{\Delta}
\begin{pmatrix}3-\alpha+\beta\\[2mm]3-\alpha+\gamma\end{pmatrix},
\]

so that  

\[
y(t)=e^{Mt}\bigl(y(0)-A\bigr)+Ae^{3t}.
\]

Writing \(c_{1}=2-A_{1},\;c_{2}=-2-A_{2}\) (with \(A_{1},A_{2}\) the components of \(A\))
gives the explicit components  

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
x_{2}(t)&=
e^{\alpha t}\Bigl(c_{1}\cosh(\omega t)+\frac{\beta c_{2}}{\omega}\sinh(\omega t)\Bigr)
+A_{1}\,e^{3t},\\[4pt]
x_{4}(t)&=
e^{\alpha t}\Bigl(c_{2}\cosh(\omega t)+\frac{\gamma c_{1}}{\omega}\sinh(\omega t)\Bigr)
+A_{2}\,e^{3t},
\end{aligned}}
\]

where  

\[
\begin{aligned}
A_{1}&=\frac{2\,(3-\alpha+\beta)}{\Delta},\qquad 
A_{2}= \frac{2\,(3-\alpha+\gamma)}{\Delta},\\[2mm]
c_{1}&=2-A_{1},\qquad 
c_{2}=-2-A_{2}.
\end{aligned}
\]

(If \(\beta\gamma=0\) one takes the limit \(\omega\to0\); then
\(\cosh(\omega t)\to1,\ \sinh(\omega t)/\omega\to t\).)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Whole solution  

Collecting the four components we obtain  

\[
\boxed{
\begin{pmatrix}
x_{1}(t)\\[2mm]
x_{2}(t)\\[2mm]
x_{3}(t)\\[2mm]
x_{4}(t)
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
e^{3t}\\[4pt]
e^{\alpha t}\Bigl(c_{1}\cosh(\omega t)+\dfrac{\beta c_{2}}{\omega}\sinh(\omega t)\Bigr)
+A_{1}e^{3t}\\[8pt]
\dfrac{(3t+2)e^{3t}+1}{(t+1)^{3}}\\[8pt]
e^{\alpha t}\Bigl(c_{2}\cosh(\omega t)+\dfrac{\gamma c_{1}}{\omega}\sinh(\omega t)\Bigr)
+A_{2}e^{3t}
\end{pmatrix}}
\]

with the constants \(A_{1},A_{2},c_{1},c_{2},\omega,\Delta\) defined above.
This satisfies the differential system and the initial condition
\(x(0)=(1,2,3,-2)^{T}\).

Solution 4:
\[
\begin{aligned}
x_{1}(t)&=e^{3t},\\[4pt]
x_{3}(t)&=\frac{(3t+2)e^{3t}+1}{(t+1)^{3}} .
\end{aligned}
\]

The remaining two components satisfy  

\[
\begin{pmatrix}x_{2}\\ x_{4}\end{pmatrix}^{\!\prime}
=
\underbrace{\begin{pmatrix}\alpha &\beta\\ \gamma &\alpha\end{pmatrix}}_{M}
\begin{pmatrix}x_{2}\\ x_{4}\end{pmatrix}
+ \underbrace{2\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 1\end{pmatrix}}_{g}\;e^{3t},
\qquad  
\begin{pmatrix}x_{2}\\ x_{4}\end{pmatrix}\!(0)=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-2\end{pmatrix}.
\]

In Problem 2 the system  

\[
y^{\prime}=My+g\,e^{3t}
\]

was solved.  Using that result we obtain the solution of the present IVP.
Put  

\[
\delta:=\sqrt{\beta\gamma},\qquad 
A:=3-\alpha,\qquad 
D:=A^{2}-\beta\gamma .
\]

(The square‑root \(\delta\) may be taken either real or complex; if \(\beta\gamma<0\) the
hyperbolic functions become trigonometric.)  
A particular solution of the non‑homogeneous system is

\[
y_{p}(t)=\frac{2}{D}
\begin{pmatrix}A+\beta\\ A+\gamma\end{pmatrix}e^{3t}.
\]

The homogeneous part is diagonalised by the eigenvalues
\(\lambda_{1}= \alpha+\delta,\;\lambda_{2}= \alpha-\delta\) with eigenvectors
\(v_{1}=(\beta,\;\delta)^{T},\;v_{2}=(\beta,\;-\delta)^{T}\).  Hence

\[
y_{h}(t)=C_{1}v_{1}e^{(\alpha+\delta)t}+C_{2}v_{2}e^{(\alpha-\delta)t}.
\]

The constants \(C_{1},C_{2}\) are found from the initial data.
Writing \(y(0)=\bigl(2,\,-2\bigr)^{T}=y_{h}(0)+y_{p}(0)\) gives

\[
\begin{cases}
\beta(C_{1}+C_{2})+\displaystyle\frac{2(A+\beta)}{D}=2,\\[6pt]
\delta(C_{1}-C_{2})+\displaystyle\frac{2(A+\gamma)}{D}=-2,
\end{cases}
\]

so that

\[
\boxed{\;
\begin{aligned}
C_{1}&=\tfrac12\Bigg[\frac{2-\tfrac{2}{D}(A+\beta)}{\beta}
+\frac{-2-\tfrac{2}{D}(A+\gamma)}{\delta}\Bigg],\\[4pt]
C_{2}&=\tfrac12\Bigg[\frac{2-\tfrac{2}{D}(A+\beta)}{\beta}
-\frac{-2-\tfrac{2}{D}(A+\gamma)}{\delta}\Bigg].
\end{aligned}}
\]

Finally

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
x_{2}(t)&=
\frac{2(A+\beta)}{D}\,e^{3t}
\;+\;\beta\Bigl(C_{1}e^{(\alpha+\delta)t}+C_{2}e^{(\alpha-\delta)t}\Bigr),\\[4pt]
x_{4}(t)&=
\frac{2(A+\gamma)}{D}\,e^{3t}
\;+\;\delta\Bigl(C_{1}e^{(\alpha+\delta)t}-C_{2}e^{(\alpha-\delta)t}\Bigr).
\end{aligned}}
\]

Equivalently, using hyperbolic functions,
\[
\begin{aligned}
x_{2}(t)&=
2e^{\alpha t}\Bigl(\cosh\!\bigl(\delta t\bigr)
-\frac{\beta}{\delta}\sinh\!\bigl(\delta t\bigr)\Bigr)
\;+\;2e^{3t}\Bigl(I_{c}(t)+\frac{\beta}{\delta}I_{s}(t)\Bigr),\\[4pt]
x_{4}(t)&=
2e^{\alpha t}\Bigl(\frac{\gamma}{\delta}\sinh\!\bigl(\delta t\bigr)
-\cosh\!\bigl(\delta t\bigr)\Bigr)
\;+\;2e^{3t}\Bigl(I_{c}(t)+\frac{\gamma}{\delta}I_{s}(t)\Bigr),
\end{aligned}
\]
with
\[
\begin{aligned}
I_{c}(t)&=\frac12\Biggl[\frac{e^{(\delta-(3-\alpha))t}-1}{\delta-(3-\alpha)}
+\frac{1-e^{-(\delta+(3-\alpha))t}}{\delta+(3-\alpha)}\Biggr],\\[4pt]
I_{s}(t)&=\frac12\Biggl[\frac{e^{(\delta-(3-\alpha))t}-1}{\delta-(3-\alpha)}
+\frac{e^{-(\delta+(3-\alpha))t}-1}{\delta+(3-\alpha)}\Biggr].
\end{aligned}
\]

All four components together give the unique solution of the initial‑value problem

\[
\boxed{
x(t)=\begin{pmatrix}
e^{3t}\\[2pt]
\displaystyle\frac{2(A+\beta)}{D}e^{3t}
+\beta\bigl(C_{1}e^{(\alpha+\delta)t}+C_{2}e^{(\alpha-\delta)t}\bigr)\\[6pt]
\displaystyle\frac{(3t+2)e^{3t}+1}{(t+1)^{3}}\\[6pt]
\displaystyle\frac{2(A+\gamma)}{D}e^{3t}
+\delta\bigl(C_{1}e^{(\alpha+\delta)t}-C_{2}e^{(\alpha-\delta)t}\bigr)
\end{pmatrix}} .
\]

This expression satisfies the differential equation and the initial condition 
\(x(0)=(1,2,3,-2)^{T}\).

Solution 5:
The system  

\[
\mathbf x'(t)=A(t)\mathbf x(t)+\mathbf f(t),\qquad   
\mathbf x(0)=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\3\\-2\end{pmatrix},
\]

with  

\[
A(t)=\begin{pmatrix}
2&0&0&0\\[2mm]
1&\alpha&0&\beta\\[2mm]
\dfrac{9}{(t+1)^2}&0&-\dfrac{3}{t+1}&0\\[2mm]
3&\gamma&0&\alpha
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad 
\mathbf f(t)=\begin{pmatrix}e^{3t}\\e^{3t}\\0\\-e^{3t}\end{pmatrix},
\]

can be solved step‑by‑step.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  The first and third components  

\[
\begin{aligned}
x_1'&=2x_1+e^{3t}, &&x_1(0)=1,\\
x_3'&=\frac{9}{(t+1)^2}x_1-\frac{3}{t+1}x_3, &&x_3(0)=3 .
\end{aligned}
\]

The first equation is independent of the others:

\[
x_1(t)=e^{3t}.
\]

Insert \(x_{1}=e^{3t}\) into the third equation:

\[
x_3'+\frac{3}{t+1}x_3 =\frac{9\,e^{3t}}{(t+1)^2}.
\]

Using the integrating factor \(\mu(t)=(t+1)^3\),

\[
\frac{d}{dt}\bigl[(t+1)^3 x_3\bigr]=9(t+1)e^{3t}.
\]

Integrating and using \(x_3(0)=3\),

\[
(t+1)^3x_3=(3t+2)e^{3t}+1,
\qquad
\boxed{\,x_3(t)=\dfrac{(3t+2)e^{3t}+1}{(t+1)^3}\,}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  The remaining two components  

Write  

\[
\mathbf y(t)=\begin{pmatrix}x_2(t)\\x_4(t)\end{pmatrix},\qquad   
\mathbf y'(t)=M\mathbf y(t)+\mathbf g(t),
\]

where  

\[
M=\begin{pmatrix}\alpha&\beta\\ \gamma&\alpha\end{pmatrix},
\qquad 
\mathbf g(t)=2e^{3t}\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad 
\mathbf y(0)=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-2\end{pmatrix}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 2.1  Homogeneous part  

\(M\) can be written as \(M=\alpha I+N\) with  

\[
N=\begin{pmatrix}0&\beta\\ \gamma&0\end{pmatrix},
\qquad N^{2}=\beta\gamma\,I .
\]

Set  

\[
\delta=\sqrt{\beta\gamma},\qquad 
D=(\alpha-3)^2-\beta\gamma .
\]

The matrix exponential of \(M\) is  

\[
e^{Mt}=e^{\alpha t}
\Bigl[ I\cosh(\delta t)+\frac{N}{\delta}\sinh(\delta t)\Bigr].
\]

Hence

\[
\mathbf y_h(t)=e^{Mt}\mathbf y(0)
      =2e^{\alpha t}\Bigl[
         \cosh(\delta t)\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix}
        -\frac{1}{\delta}\sinh(\delta t)
          \begin{pmatrix}\beta\\-\gamma\end{pmatrix}
        \Bigr].
\tag{2.1}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 2.2  Particular part  

Variation of constants gives  

\[
\mathbf y_p(t)=\int_{0}^{t} e^{M(t-s)}\mathbf g(s)\,ds
              =2e^{3t}\int_{0}^{t}e^{(M-3I)u}\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}du,
\quad u=t-s .
\]

Because  

\[
e^{(M-3I)u}=e^{(\alpha-3)u}
\Bigl[I\cosh(\delta u)+\frac{N}{\delta}\sinh(\delta u)\Bigr],
\]

the integrand acting on \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}\) becomes  

\[
e^{(\alpha-3)u}\Bigl[
\cosh(\delta u)\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}
+\frac{\sinh(\delta u)}{\delta}
\begin{pmatrix}\beta\\\gamma\end{pmatrix}\Bigr].
\]

The needed scalar integrals are  

\[
\begin{aligned}
I_{1}(t)&=\int_{0}^{t}e^{(\alpha-3)u}\cosh(\delta u)\,du
        =\frac{e^{(\alpha-3)t}\bigl((\alpha-3)\cosh\delta t+\delta\sinh\delta t\bigr)-(\alpha-3)}{D},\\[4pt]
I_{2}(t)&=\int_{0}^{t}e^{(\alpha-3)u}\sinh(\delta u)\,du
        =\frac{e^{(\alpha-3)t}\bigl((\alpha-3)\sinh\delta t+\delta\cosh\delta t\bigr)-\delta}{D}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Consequently  

\[
\boxed{\;
\mathbf y_{p}(t)=2e^{3t}
\begin{pmatrix}
 I_{1}(t)+\dfrac{\beta}{\delta}\,I_{2}(t)\\[6pt]
 I_{1}(t)+\dfrac{\gamma}{\delta}\,I_{2}(t)
\end{pmatrix}
\; } .
\tag{2.2}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Complete solution  

Collecting the four components,

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
x_{1}(t)&=e^{3t},\\[4pt]
x_{2}(t)&=2e^{\alpha t}\Bigl[\cosh(\delta t)-\frac{\beta}{\delta}\sinh(\delta t)\Bigr]
          +2e^{3t}\Bigl[I_{1}(t)+\frac{\beta}{\delta}I_{2}(t)\Bigr],\\[6pt]
x_{3}(t)&=\displaystyle\frac{(3t+2)e^{3t}+1}{(t+1)^{3}},\\[12pt]
x_{4}(t)&=2e^{\alpha t}\Bigl[-\cosh(\delta t)+\frac{\gamma}{\delta}\sinh(\delta t)\Bigr]
          +2e^{3t}\Bigl[I_{1}(t)+\frac{\gamma}{\delta}I_{2}(t)\Bigr],
\end{aligned}}
\]

with  

\[
\delta=\sqrt{\beta\gamma},\qquad 
D=(\alpha-3)^{2}-\beta\gamma,
\]

\[
\begin{aligned}
I_{1}(t)&=\frac{e^{(\alpha-3)t}\bigl((\alpha-3)\cosh(\delta t)+\delta\sinh(\delta t)\bigr)-(\alpha-3)}{D},\\[4pt]
I_{2}(t)&=\frac{e^{(\alpha-3)t}\bigl((\alpha-3)\sinh(\delta t)+\delta\cosh(\delta t)\bigr)-\delta}{D}.
\end{aligned}
\]

(When \(\beta\gamma=0\) the formulas are obtained by taking the limit \(\delta\to0\); the same result follows from the nilpotent case \(N^{2}=0\).)

These expressions satisfy the differential system and the initial condition, completing the solution of the IVP. \boxed{}

Solution 6:
The first equation is decoupled from the rest, so we solve it first  

\[
x'_1=2x_1+e^{3t},\qquad x_1(0)=1 .
\]

With the integrating factor \(e^{-2t}\),

\[
\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(e^{-2t}x_1\bigr)=e^{t}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad 
x_1(t)=C e^{2t}+e^{3t}.
\]

Using \(x_1(0)=1\) gives \(C=0\); hence  

\[
\boxed{x_1(t)=e^{3t}} .
\]

---

### The third component  

\[
x'_3=\frac{9}{(t+1)^2}x_1-\frac{3}{t+1}x_3
      =\frac{9}{(t+1)^2}e^{3t}-\frac{3}{t+1}x_3,
\qquad x_3(0)=3 .
\]

Write the equation in standard linear form  

\[
x'_3+\frac{3}{t+1}x_3=\frac{9}{(t+1)^2}e^{3t}.
\]

The integrating factor is \(\mu(t)=(t+1)^3\). Multiplying by \(\mu\) we obtain  

\[
\frac{d}{dt}\bigl((t+1)^3x_3\bigr)=9(t+1)e^{3t}.
\]

Integrating from \(0\) to \(t\),

\[
(t+1)^3x_3=(3t+2)e^{3t}+C .
\]

Because \((1)^3x_3(0)=3\),

\[
C=3-(2)=1.
\]

Thus  

\[
\boxed{\,x_3(t)=\frac{(3t+2)e^{3t}+1}{(t+1)^3}\,}.
\]

---

### The second and fourth components  

With \(x_1(t)=e^{3t}\) the remaining equations become  

\[
\begin{aligned}
x'_2 &= e^{3t}+ \alpha x_2+\beta x_4+e^{3t}
      =\alpha x_2+\beta x_4+2e^{3t},\\[2mm]
x'_4 &= 3e^{3t}+ \gamma x_2+\alpha x_4-e^{3t}
      =\gamma x_2+\alpha x_4+2e^{3t},
\end{aligned}
\qquad 
\begin{pmatrix}x_2(0)\\x_4(0)\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-2\end{pmatrix}.
\]

In Problem 2 the homogeneous system  

\[
\mathbf y' = 
\begin{pmatrix}\alpha & \beta\\ \gamma & \alpha\end{pmatrix}\mathbf y
\]

was solved, and its fundamental matrix was shown to be  

\[
e^{Bt}=e^{\alpha t}
\begin{pmatrix}
\cosh(\sqrt{\beta\gamma}\,t) & \dfrac{\beta}{\sqrt{\beta\gamma}}\sinh(\sqrt{\beta\gamma}\,t)\\[4pt]
\dfrac{\gamma}{\sqrt{\beta\gamma}}\sinh(\sqrt{\beta\gamma}\,t) & \cosh(\sqrt{\beta\gamma}\,t)
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
B=\begin{pmatrix}\alpha&\beta\\ \gamma&\alpha\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Using the variation‑of‑constants formula we obtain  

\[
\begin{pmatrix}x_2(t)\\x_4(t)\end{pmatrix}
= e^{Bt}\begin{pmatrix}2\\-2\end{pmatrix}
+2\int_{0}^{t}e^{B(t-s)}e^{3s}\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}\,ds .
\]

When the constants are taken as \(\alpha=\beta=\gamma=0\) (the case treated in Problem 2), the matrix exponential reduces to the identity and the integral is elementary:

\[
\begin{aligned}
x_2(t)&=2+\int_{0}^{t}2e^{3s}\,ds
      =2+\frac{2}{3}\bigl(e^{3t}-1\bigr)
      =\frac{2}{3}e^{3t}+\frac{4}{3},\\[4pt]
x_4(t)&=-2+\int_{0}^{t}2e^{3s}\,ds
      =-2+\frac{2}{3}\bigl(e^{3t}-1\bigr)
      =\frac{2}{3}e^{3t}-\frac{8}{3}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Both satisfy the given initial conditions \(x_2(0)=2,\;x_4(0)=-2\).

---

### Complete solution  

Collecting the four components, the solution of the IVP is  

\[
\boxed{
x(t)=\begin{pmatrix}
e^{3t}\\[4pt]
\dfrac{2}{3}e^{3t}+\dfrac{4}{3}\\[6pt]
\dfrac{(3t+2)e^{3t}+1}{(t+1)^3}\\[8pt]
\dfrac{2}{3}e^{3t}-\dfrac{8}{3}
\end{pmatrix}}
\]

which indeed satisfies \(x'(t)=A(t)x(t)+f(t)\) and the initial condition \(x(0)=(1,2,3,-2)^{\!T}\).  (If \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\) are non‑zero, one replaces the explicit formulas for \(x_2\) and \(x_4\) by the variation‑of‑constants expression displayed above.)

Solution 7:
The system can be solved component–wise because the first and the third equations are already decoupled and the second–fourth equations form a \(2\times2\) autonomous linear subsystem.  

---

### 1.  The first component  

\[
x_1'=2x_1+e^{3t},\qquad x_1(0)=1 .
\]

\[
x_1(t)=e^{3t}.
\]

---

### 2.  The third component  

\[
x_3'=\frac{9}{(t+1)^2}x_1-\frac{3}{t+1}x_3 ,\qquad x_3(0)=3 .
\]

With \(x_1(t)=e^{3t}\) this linear equation has the integrating factor \((t+1)^3\) and

\[
(t+1)^3x_3(t)=\int_0^t 9e^{3s}(s+1)\,ds+3
           =(3t+2)e^{3t}+1 .
\]

Hence  

\[
\boxed{\,x_3(t)=\displaystyle\frac{(3t+2)e^{3t}+1}{(t+1)^3}\, } .
\]

---

### 3.  The subsystem \((x_2,x_4)\)

Write  

\[
y(t)=\begin{pmatrix}x_2(t)\\x_4(t)\end{pmatrix},
\qquad 
y' = My+2e^{3t}\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad 
M=\begin{pmatrix}\alpha&\beta\\ \gamma&\alpha\end{pmatrix},
\qquad 
y(0)=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-2\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Let  

\[
\lambda:=\sqrt{\beta\gamma}\qquad(\lambda=0\ \hbox{if } \beta\gamma=0).
\]

Because \(M=\alpha I+N\) with \(N^2=\beta\gamma I=\lambda^{2}I\), the matrix exponential is  

\[
e^{Mt}=e^{\alpha t}\Bigl(
I\cosh(\lambda t)+\frac{N}{\lambda}\sinh(\lambda t)\Bigr) ,
\qquad 
\Bigl(\frac{N}{\lambda}=0\;{\rm when}\;\lambda=0\Bigr).
\]

Thus a fundamental matrix for the homogeneous subsystem is  

\[
\Phi(t)=e^{\alpha t}
\begin{pmatrix}
\cosh(\lambda t)&\displaystyle\frac{\beta}{\lambda}\sinh(\lambda t)\\[6pt]
\displaystyle\frac{\gamma}{\lambda}\sinh(\lambda t)&\cosh(\lambda t)
\end{pmatrix}
\qquad(\Phi(0)=I).
\]

Using variation of parameters,

\[
y(t)=\Phi(t)y(0)+2\int_{0}^{t}\Phi(t)\Phi(s)^{-1}e^{3s}
        \begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}ds .
\]

Since \(\Phi(s)^{-1}=e^{-\alpha s}
\bigl(I\cosh(\lambda s)-\frac{N}{\lambda}\sinh(\lambda s)\bigr)\), a short computation gives

\[
\begin{aligned}
y(t)&=e^{\alpha t}
\Bigl[\cosh(\lambda t)I+\frac{N}{\lambda}\sinh(\lambda t)\Bigr]
\begin{pmatrix}2\\-2\end{pmatrix}
\\[2mm]
&\quad\; +2e^{3t}\Bigl\{
\frac{1}{2}
\Bigl[\frac{1+\frac{\beta}{\lambda}}{\,3-(\alpha+\lambda)}\bigl(1-e^{-(3-(\alpha+\lambda))t}\bigr)
      +\frac{1-\frac{\beta}{\lambda}}{\,3-(\alpha-\lambda)}\bigl(1-e^{-(3-(\alpha-\lambda))t}\bigr)\Bigr]
\!\\[1mm]
&\qquad\qquad\qquad\;
\begin{pmatrix}
1\\
\displaystyle\frac{\gamma}{\beta}
\end{pmatrix}
\Bigl\}\!.
\end{aligned}
\]

Writing the two components explicitly, and using \(\lambda=\sqrt{\beta\gamma}\),

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
x_2(t)&=
e^{\alpha t}\bigl[\,2\cosh(\lambda t)-\tfrac{2\beta}{\lambda}\sinh(\lambda t)\bigr] \\
&\qquad+2e^{3t}\Biggl[
\frac{1+\frac{\beta}{\lambda}}{\,3-(\alpha+\lambda)}\Bigl(1-e^{-(3-(\alpha+\lambda))t}\Bigr)
+\frac{1-\frac{\beta}{\lambda}}{\,3-(\alpha-\lambda)}\Bigl(1-e^{-(3-(\alpha-\lambda))t}\Bigr)
\Biggr],\\[4mm]
x_4(t)&=
e^{\alpha t}\bigl[-2\cosh(\lambda t)+\tfrac{2\gamma}{\lambda}\sinh(\lambda t)\bigr] \\
&\qquad+2e^{3t}\Biggl[
\frac{1+\frac{\gamma}{\lambda}}{\,3-(\alpha+\lambda)}\Bigl(1-e^{-(3-(\alpha+\lambda))t}\Bigr)
+\frac{1-\frac{\gamma}{\lambda}}{\,3-(\alpha-\lambda)}\Bigl(1-e^{-(3-(\alpha-\lambda))t}\Bigr)
\Biggr] .
\end{aligned}}
\]

(The formulas remain valid when \(\beta\gamma=0\) after the obvious limits \(\lambda\to0\), \(\cosh(\lambda t)\to1\), \(\sinh(\lambda t)/\lambda\to t\).)

---

### 4.  The complete solution

Collecting the four components we obtain the solution of the initial‑value problem:

\[
\boxed{
\begin{pmatrix}
x_1(t)\\[2mm]x_2(t)\\[2mm]x_3(t)\\[2mm]x_4(t)
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
e^{3t}\\[2mm]
\displaystyle e^{\alpha t}\bigl[2\cosh(\lambda t)-\tfrac{2\beta}{\lambda}\sinh(\lambda t)\bigr]
      +2e^{3t}\Bigl[\frac{1+\beta/\lambda}{3-(\alpha+\lambda)}\!\bigl(1-e^{-(3-(\alpha+\lambda))t}\bigr)
                     +\frac{1-\beta/\lambda}{3-(\alpha-\lambda)}\!\bigl(1-e^{-(3-(\alpha-\lambda))t}\bigr)\Bigr]\\[4mm]
\displaystyle\frac{(3t+2)e^{3t}+1}{(t+1)^3}\\[4mm]
\displaystyle e^{\alpha t}\bigl[-2\cosh(\lambda t)+\tfrac{2\gamma}{\lambda}\sinh(\lambda t)\bigr]
      +2e^{3t}\Bigl[\frac{1+\gamma/\lambda}{3-(\alpha+\lambda)}\!\bigl(1-e^{-(3-(\alpha+\lambda))t}\bigr)
                     +\frac{1-\gamma/\lambda}{3-(\alpha-\lambda)}\!\bigl(1-e^{-(3-(\alpha-\lambda))t}\bigr)\Bigr]
\end{pmatrix}}
\]

with \(\displaystyle\lambda=\sqrt{\beta\gamma}\) (and the limiting forms when \(\beta\gamma=0\)).  This vector satisfies the given differential system and the initial condition \(x(0)=(1,2,3,-2)^T\).

Solution 8:
\[
\begin{aligned}
x_1'(t)&=2x_1(t)+e^{3t}, &
x_2'(t)&=x_1(t)+\alpha x_2(t)+\beta x_4(t)+e^{3t},\\
x_3'(t)&=\frac{9}{(t+1)^2}x_1(t)-\frac{3}{t+1}x_3(t), &
x_4'(t)&=3x_1(t)+\gamma x_2(t)+\alpha x_4(t)-e^{3t},
\end{aligned}
\qquad 
x(0)=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\3\\-2\end{pmatrix}.
\]

The first equation is autonomous and gives  

\[
\boxed{x_1(t)=e^{3t}} .
\]

---

### The third component  

\[
x_3'+\frac{3}{t+1}x_3=\frac{9\,e^{3t}}{(t+1)^2},
\qquad 
\mu(t)=(t+1)^3 .
\]

Hence  

\[
\frac{d}{dt}\bigl[(t+1)^3x_3(t)\bigr]=9e^{3t}(t+1)
\]

and, using \(x_3(0)=3\),

\[
(t+1)^3x_3(t)=3+9\int_0^{t}e^{3s}(s+1)\,ds
           =1+e^{3t}(3t+2).
\]

Therefore  

\[
\boxed{x_3(t)=\dfrac{1+e^{3t}(3t+2)}{(t+1)^3}}\; .
\]

---

### The \((x_2,x_4)\)-subsystem  

Write  

\[
\mathbf y(t)=\begin{pmatrix}x_2(t)\\x_4(t)\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\mathbf y' =M\mathbf y+2e^{3t}\mathbf v,\qquad 
M=\begin{pmatrix}\alpha&\beta\\\gamma&\alpha\end{pmatrix},
\;\;\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}.
\]

A constant‑particular solution \(\mathbf y_p(t)=\mathbf c\,e^{3t}\) is obtained from  

\[
(3I-M)\mathbf c=2\mathbf v .
\]

Writing   

\[
\Delta:=(3-\alpha)^2-\beta\gamma,\qquad 
\mathbf c=\begin{pmatrix}A\\B\end{pmatrix}
        =\frac{2}{\Delta}
          \begin{pmatrix}(3-\alpha)+\beta\\(3-\alpha)+\gamma\end{pmatrix},
\tag{1}
\]

the homogeneous solution uses the matrix exponential of \(M\).  
Because  

\[
M=\alpha I+N,\qquad 
N=\begin{pmatrix}0&\beta\\\gamma&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad 
N^2=\beta\gamma\,I,
\]

set  

\[
D:=\sqrt{\beta\gamma}\qquad(\text{take the principal branch}).
\]

If \(D\neq0\),

\[
e^{Mt}=e^{\alpha t}\Bigl(\cosh(Dt)I+\frac{\sinh(Dt)}{D}N\Bigr).
\tag{2}
\]

If \(\beta\gamma=0\) the limit of (2) gives \(e^{Mt}=e^{\alpha t}(I+Nt)\).

Let  

\[
\mathbf C:=\mathbf y(0)-\mathbf c
         =\begin{pmatrix}2\\-2\end{pmatrix}
          -\begin{pmatrix}A\\B\end{pmatrix}
         =\begin{pmatrix}C_2\\C_4\end{pmatrix},
\qquad 
C_2=2-A,\;C_4=-2-B .
\]

The general solution of the subsystem is  

\[
\mathbf y(t)=e^{Mt}\mathbf C+\mathbf c\,e^{3t}.
\tag{3}
\]

Using (2) and (3) we obtain the explicit formulas

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
x_2(t)&=e^{\alpha t}
\Bigl[\,C_2\cosh(Dt)+\frac{\beta C_4}{D}\sinh(Dt)\Bigr]
      +A\,e^{3t},\\[4pt]
x_4(t)&=e^{\alpha t}
\Bigl[\,C_4\cosh(Dt)+\frac{\gamma C_2}{D}\sinh(Dt)\Bigr]
      +B\,e^{3t},
\end{aligned}}
\qquad(D\neq0)
\]

and in the degenerate case \(\beta\gamma=0\),

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
x_2(t)&=e^{\alpha t}\bigl(C_2+\beta C_4\,t\bigr)+A\,e^{3t},\\[4pt]
x_4(t)&=e^{\alpha t}\bigl(C_4+\gamma C_2\,t\bigr)+B\,e^{3t}.
\end{aligned}}
\]

All the constants appearing above are expressed through the given parameters  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\Delta&=(3-\alpha)^2-\beta\gamma,\\
A&=\dfrac{2\bigl((3-\alpha)+\beta\bigr)}{\Delta},\qquad
B=\dfrac{2\bigl((3-\alpha)+\gamma\bigr)}{\Delta},\\[4pt]
C_2&=2-A,\qquad
C_4=-2-B,\\[4pt]
D&=\sqrt{\beta\gamma}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Finally, collecting all four components we have the solution of the initial–value problem

\[
\boxed{
x(t)=\begin{pmatrix}
e^{3t}\\[4pt]
e^{\alpha t}\Bigl[\,C_2\cosh(Dt)+\frac{\beta C_4}{D}\sinh(Dt)\Bigr]+A\,e^{3t}\\[4pt]
\dfrac{1+e^{3t}(3t+2)}{(t+1)^3}\\[10pt]
e^{\alpha t}\Bigl[\,C_4\cosh(Dt)+\frac{\gamma C_2}{D}\sinh(Dt)\Bigr]+B\,e^{3t}
\end{pmatrix}}
\]

(if \(\beta\gamma=0\) replace the hyperbolic terms by their limits as indicated above).  This vector satisfies the differential system and the initial condition \(x(0)=(1,2,3,-2)^T\).

Solution 9:
The system can be written componentwise as  

\[
\begin{aligned}
x_1' &=2x_1+e^{3t},\\[2mm]
x_2' &=x_1+\alpha x_2+\beta x_4+e^{3t},\\[2mm]
x_3' &=\frac{9}{(t+1)^2}x_1-\frac{3}{t+1}x_3,\\[2mm]
x_4' &=3x_1+\gamma x_2+\alpha x_4-e^{3t},
\end{aligned}
\qquad 
x(0)=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\3\\-2\end{pmatrix}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Solving for \(x_{1}\) and \(x_{3}\)

\(x_{1}\) satisfies a scalar linear ODE  

\[
x_1'-2x_1=e^{3t}\;,
\qquad x_1(0)=1,
\]

hence  

\[
\boxed{x_1(t)=e^{3t}} .
\]

\(x_{3}\) obeys  

\[
x_3'+\frac{3}{t+1}x_3=\frac{9}{(t+1)^2}x_1
            =\frac{9}{(t+1)^2}e^{3t},
\qquad x_3(0)=3 .
\]

With the integrating factor \((t+1)^3\) we obtain  

\[
(t+1)^3x_3 =\int 9(t+1)e^{3t}\,dt+(t+1)^3C
           =(3t+2)e^{3t}+C .
\]

Using \(x_3(0)=3\) gives \(C=1\); therefore  

\[
\boxed{\,x_3(t)=\frac{(3t+2)e^{3t}+1}{(t+1)^3}\,}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  The subsystem for \(x_{2},x_{4}\)

Insert \(x_{1}=e^{3t}\) into the remaining equations:

\[
\begin{cases}
x_2' = 2e^{3t}+\alpha x_2+\beta x_4,\\[2mm]
x_4' = 2e^{3t}+\gamma x_2+\alpha x_4 .
\end{cases}
\tag{1}
\]

Write \(y=(x_2,x_4)^{T}\).  Then  

\[
y' = My+g(t),\qquad 
M=\begin{pmatrix}\alpha &\beta\\ \gamma &\alpha\end{pmatrix},
\qquad 
g(t)=2e^{3t}\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Homogeneous part

The eigen‑values of \(M\) are  

\[
\lambda_{1,2}= \alpha\pm s,\qquad 
s:=\sqrt{\beta\gamma}.
\]

Corresponding eigenvectors are  

\[
v_1=\begin{pmatrix}\sqrt{\beta}\\ \sqrt{\gamma}\end{pmatrix},
\qquad 
v_2=\begin{pmatrix}\sqrt{\beta}\\ -\sqrt{\gamma}\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Hence the fundamental matrix of the homogeneous system is  

\[
\Phi(t)=\bigl[\,v_1e^{\lambda_1t},\;v_2e^{\lambda_2t}\,\bigr]
      =\begin{pmatrix}
        \sqrt{\beta}e^{\lambda_1t}&\sqrt{\beta}e^{\lambda_2t}\\[2mm]
        \sqrt{\gamma}e^{\lambda_1t}&-\sqrt{\gamma}e^{\lambda_2t}
        \end{pmatrix}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Particular solution (variation of parameters)

\[
\Phi(t)^{-1}= 
\begin{pmatrix}
\displaystyle\frac{e^{-(\alpha+s)t}}{2\sqrt{\beta}} &
\displaystyle\frac{e^{-(\alpha+s)t}}{2\sqrt{\gamma}}\\[4mm]
\displaystyle\frac{e^{(-\alpha+s)t}}{2\sqrt{\beta}} &
\displaystyle-\frac{e^{-(\alpha-s)t}}{2\sqrt{\gamma}}
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Therefore  

\[
\Phi(t)^{-1}g(t)=
2e^{3t}\begin{pmatrix}
\displaystyle\frac{\sqrt{\beta}+\sqrt{\gamma}}{\sqrt{\beta\gamma}}
          e^{-(\alpha+s)t}\\[4mm]
\displaystyle\frac{-\sqrt{\beta}+\sqrt{\gamma}}{\sqrt{\beta\gamma}}
          e^{-(\alpha-s)t}
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Integrating,

\[
\int\Phi^{-1}g\,dt=
\begin{pmatrix}
\displaystyle\frac{\sqrt{\beta}+\sqrt{\gamma}}{\sqrt{\beta\gamma}}
      \frac{e^{(3-\alpha-s)t}}{3-\alpha-s}\\[6mm]
\displaystyle\frac{-\sqrt{\beta}+\sqrt{\gamma}}{\sqrt{\beta\gamma}}
      \frac{e^{(3-\alpha+s)t}}{3-\alpha+s}
\end{pmatrix}+C .
\]

Multiplying by \(\Phi(t)\) and simplifying gives a particular solution that is
proportional to \(e^{3t}\):

\[
y_p(t)=\frac{2(\beta-\alpha+3)}{(\alpha-3)^2-\beta\gamma}\;e^{3t}
        \begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  General solution of the subsystem

\[
y(t)=\Phi(t)C_0+y_p(t),\qquad 
C_0=\begin{pmatrix}C_1\\C_2\end{pmatrix},
\]

i.e.

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
x_2(t)&=
\sqrt{\beta}\bigl(C_1e^{(\alpha+s)t}+C_2e^{(\alpha-s)t}\bigr)
+\frac{2(\beta-\alpha+3)}{(\alpha-3)^2-\beta\gamma}\,e^{3t},\\[4pt]
x_4(t)&=
\sqrt{\gamma}\bigl(C_1e^{(\alpha+s)t}-C_2e^{(\alpha-s)t}\bigr)
+\frac{2(\beta-\alpha+3)}{(\alpha-3)^2-\beta\gamma}\,e^{3t}.
\end{aligned}}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 6.  Determining the constants from the initial data

At \(t=0\),

\[
\begin{cases}
\sqrt{\beta}(C_1+C_2)+P =2,\\[2mm]
\sqrt{\gamma}(C_1-C_2)+P =-2,
\end{cases}
\qquad 
P:=\dfrac{2(\beta-\alpha+3)}{(\alpha-3)^2-\beta\gamma}.
\]

Solving,

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
C_1&=\frac{-P(\sqrt{\beta}+\sqrt{\gamma})-2\sqrt{\beta}+2\sqrt{\gamma}}
         {2\sqrt{\beta\gamma}},\\[4pt]
C_2&=\frac{\,P(\sqrt{\beta}-\sqrt{\gamma})+2\sqrt{\beta}+2\sqrt{\gamma}}
         {2\sqrt{\beta\gamma}}.
\end{aligned}}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 7.  Complete solution of the original IVP

Collecting the four components, the solution of the initial‑value problem is  

\[
\boxed{
x(t)=\begin{pmatrix}
e^{3t}\\[4pt]
\displaystyle\sqrt{\beta}\bigl(C_1e^{(\alpha+\sqrt{\beta\gamma})t}
                               +C_2e^{(\alpha-\sqrt{\beta\gamma})t}\bigr)
   +\dfrac{2(\beta-\alpha+3)}{(\alpha-3)^2-\beta\gamma}\,e^{3t}\\[12pt]
\displaystyle\frac{(3t+2)e^{3t}+1}{(t+1)^3}\\[12pt]
\displaystyle\sqrt{\gamma}\bigl(C_1e^{(\alpha+\sqrt{\beta\gamma})t}
                               -C_2e^{(\alpha-\sqrt{\beta\gamma})t}\bigr)
   +\dfrac{2(\beta-\alpha+3)}{(\alpha-3)^2-\beta\gamma}\,e^{3t}
\end{pmatrix}}
\]

where  

\[
C_1=\frac{-P(\sqrt{\beta}+\sqrt{\gamma})-2\sqrt{\beta}+2\sqrt{\gamma}}
         {2\sqrt{\beta\gamma}},\qquad
C_2=\frac{P(\sqrt{\beta}-\sqrt{\gamma})+2\sqrt{\beta}+2\sqrt{\gamma}}
         {2\sqrt{\beta\gamma}},\qquad
P=\frac{2(\beta-\alpha+3)}{(\alpha-3)^2-\beta\gamma}.
\]

This vector satisfies the differential system and the initial condition
\(x(0)=(1,2,3,-2)^{T}\).

Solution 10:
**Step 1 – the first and the third components**

The first equation is decoupled  

\[
x_1' = 2x_1+e^{3t},\qquad x_1(0)=1 .
\]

Its solution is obtained by an integrating factor:

\[
x_1(t)=e^{2t}\Big(\int_0^t e^{-2s}e^{3s}\,ds+1\Big)
      =e^{2t}\big(e^{t}-0\big)=e^{3t}.
\]

The third equation is linear in \(x_3\) once \(x_1\) is known:

\[
x_3' +\frac{3}{t+1}x_3=\frac{9}{(t+1)^2}e^{3t},
\qquad x_3(0)=3 .
\]

The integrating factor is \(\mu(t)=(t+1)^3\).  Hence  

\[
\frac{d}{dt}\Big((t+1)^3x_3\Big)=9(t+1)e^{3t}
\]

and, after integration,

\[
(t+1)^3x_3(t)=\big(3t+2\big)e^{3t}+1 .
\]

Thus  

\[
\boxed{x_3(t)=\dfrac{(3t+2)e^{3t}+1}{(t+1)^3}} .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

**Step 2 – the subsystem for \((x_2,x_4)\)**  

Put  

\[
y(t):=\begin{pmatrix}x_2(t)\\x_4(t)\end{pmatrix},\qquad 
M:=\begin{pmatrix}\alpha&\beta\\ \gamma&\alpha\end{pmatrix},
\qquad g(t)=2e^{3t}\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}.
\]

From the second and fourth rows of the original system we obtain  

\[
y'(t)=My(t)+g(t), \qquad 
y(0)=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-2\end{pmatrix}.
\tag{1}
\]

Write \(M=\alpha I+N\) with  

\[
N=\begin{pmatrix}0&\beta\\ \gamma&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad 
N^2=\beta\gamma\, I .
\]

Set  

\[
\delta:=\sqrt{\beta\gamma}\qquad(\text{the principal square root}).
\]

Because \(N\) commutes with itself,  

\[
e^{Mt}=e^{\alpha t}\Big(I\cosh(\delta t)+\frac{N}{\delta}\sinh(\delta t)\Big).
\tag{2}
\]

Using the variation‑of‑constants formula for (1),

\[
y(t)=e^{Mt}y(0)+\int_0^t e^{M(t-s)}\,g(s)\,ds .
\tag{3}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
**Step 3 – evaluation of the integral**

From (2) and \(g(s)=2e^{3s}(1,1)^T\),

\[
e^{M(t-s)}g(s)=2e^{3s}e^{\alpha (t-s)}\Big(
   \cosh[\delta (t-s)]\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}
   +\frac{\sinh[\delta (t-s)]}{\delta}
      \begin{pmatrix}\beta\\\gamma\end{pmatrix}\Big).
\]

Hence the integral appearing in (3) can be written as  

\[
2e^{3t}\Big[
   I_{1}(t)\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}
   +\frac{I_{2}(t)}{\delta}\begin{pmatrix}\beta\\\gamma\end{pmatrix}\Big],
\]

where  

\[
\begin{aligned}
I_{1}(t)&:=\int_{0}^{t}e^{-(3-\alpha)u}\cosh(\delta u)\,du,\\[2mm]
I_{2}(t)&:=\int_{0}^{t}e^{-(3-\alpha)u}\sinh(\delta u)\,du .
\end{aligned}
\]

Evaluating the two elementary integrals gives  

\[
\begin{aligned}
I_{1}(t)&=\frac12\Big(
   \frac{e^{(\alpha+\delta-3)t}-1}{\alpha+\delta-3}
 + \frac{e^{(\alpha-\delta-3)t}-1}{\alpha-\delta-3}\Big),\\[2mm]
I_{2}(t)&=\frac12\Big(
   \frac{e^{(\alpha+\delta-3)t}-1}{\alpha+\delta-3}
 - \frac{e^{(\alpha-\delta-3)t}-1}{\alpha-\delta-3}\Big).
\end{aligned}
\tag{4}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
**Step 4 – the explicit components \(x_2,x_4\)**  

Insert the expressions (2) and (4) into (3).  After a short simplification we obtain

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
x_{2}(t)&=e^{\alpha t}\Big(2\cosh(\delta t)-\frac{2\beta}{\delta}\sinh(\delta t)\Big)\\
&\qquad+2e^{3t}\Big[
     \frac{(1+\beta/\delta)\big(e^{(\alpha+\delta-3)t}-1\big)}{2(\alpha+\delta-3)}
   + \frac{(1-\beta/\delta)\big(e^{(\alpha-\delta-3)t}-1\big)}{2(\alpha-\delta-3)}
   \Big],
\\[4pt]
x_{4}(t)&=e^{\alpha t}\Big(-2\cosh(\delta t)+\frac{2\gamma}{\delta}\sinh(\delta t)\Big)\\
&\qquad+2e^{3t}\Big[
     \frac{(1+\gamma/\delta)\big(e^{(\alpha+\delta-3)t}-1\big)}{2(\alpha+\delta-3)}
   + \frac{(1-\gamma/\delta)\big(e^{(\alpha-\delta-3)t}-1\big)}{2(\alpha-\delta-3)}
   \Big],
\end{aligned}}
\]

with \(\displaystyle\delta=\sqrt{\beta\gamma}\) (if \(\beta\gamma=0\) the formulas are obtained by taking the limit \(\delta\to0\)).  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
**Step 5 – the complete solution**

Collecting the four components we finally have

\[
\boxed{
\begin{pmatrix}
x_{1}(t)\\[4pt] x_{2}(t)\\[4pt] x_{3}(t)\\[4pt] x_{4}(t)
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
e^{3t}\\[4pt]
\displaystyle e^{\alpha t}\Big(2\cosh(\sqrt{\beta\gamma}\,t)-\frac{2\beta}{\sqrt{\beta\gamma}}\sinh(\sqrt{\beta\gamma}\,t)\Big)
+2e^{3t}\Big[
 \frac{(1+\beta/\sqrt{\beta\gamma})\big(e^{(\alpha+\sqrt{\beta\gamma}-3)t}-1\big)}{2(\alpha+\sqrt{\beta\gamma}-3)}
+\frac{(1-\beta/\sqrt{\beta\gamma})\big(e^{(\alpha-\sqrt{\beta\gamma}-3)t}-1\big)}{2(\alpha-\sqrt{\beta\gamma}-3)}
\Big]\\[12pt]
\displaystyle\frac{(3t+2)e^{3t}+1}{(t+1)^3}\\[12pt]
\displaystyle e^{\alpha t}\Big(-2\cosh(\sqrt{\beta\gamma}\,t)+\frac{2\gamma}{\sqrt{\beta\gamma}}\sinh(\sqrt{\beta\gamma}\,t)\Big)
+2e^{3t}\Big[
 \frac{(1+\gamma/\sqrt{\beta\gamma})\big(e^{(\alpha+\sqrt{\beta\gamma}-3)t}-1\big)}{2(\alpha+\sqrt{\beta\gamma}-3)}
+\frac{(1-\gamma/\sqrt{\beta\gamma})\big(e^{(\alpha-\sqrt{\beta\gamma}-3)t}-1\big)}{2(\alpha-\sqrt{\beta\gamma}-3)}
\Big]
\end{pmatrix}}
\]

which satisfies the given initial condition \(x(0)=(1,2,3,-2)^T\).  (For the degenerate case \(\beta\gamma=0\) replace the hyperbolic‑function terms by their limits.)

Solution 11:
\[
\begin{aligned}
x_1(t)&=e^{3t},\\[4pt]
x_3(t)&=\frac{(3t+2)e^{3t}+1}{(t+1)^3},
\end{aligned}
\]

and the remaining two components are obtained from the \(2\times 2\) subsystem  

\[
\begin{pmatrix}x_2\\ x_4\end{pmatrix}'=
\begin{pmatrix}\alpha &\beta\\ \gamma &\alpha\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}x_2\\ x_4\end{pmatrix}
+2e^{3t}\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad 
\begin{pmatrix}x_2\\ x_4\end{pmatrix}(0)=
\begin{pmatrix}2\\-2\end{pmatrix}.
\]

---

### 1.  Particular solution  

Seek a particular solution of the form \(\displaystyle 
\begin{pmatrix}x_2\\ x_4\end{pmatrix}_p=k\,e^{3t}\) with a constant vector
\(k=(k_1,k_2)^{\!T}\). Substituting gives  

\[
(3I-A)k=2\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad 
A=\begin{pmatrix}\alpha &\beta\\ \gamma &\alpha\end{pmatrix},
\]

so that  

\[
\boxed{
k=
\begin{pmatrix}
\displaystyle\frac{-2\alpha+2\beta+6}
{\alpha^{2}-6\alpha-\beta\gamma+9}\\[8pt]
\displaystyle\frac{-2\alpha+2\gamma+6}
{\alpha^{2}-6\alpha-\beta\gamma+9}
\end{pmatrix}}.
\tag{1}
\]

Hence  

\[
\begin{pmatrix}x_2\\ x_4\end{pmatrix}_p=
k\,e^{3t}.
\]

---

### 2.  Homogeneous solution  

Write \(A=\alpha I+N\) with  

\[
N=\begin{pmatrix}0&\beta\\ \gamma&0\end{pmatrix},
\qquad 
N^{2}=\beta\gamma\,I .
\]

Let \(\displaystyle\delta=\sqrt{\beta\gamma}\) (we assume \(\beta\gamma\neq0\); the
case \(\beta\gamma=0\) follows by continuity).  
Using the series for the matrix exponential,

\[
e^{At}=e^{\alpha t}
\Bigl[I\cosh(\delta t)+\frac{N}{\delta}\sinh(\delta t)\Bigr].
\tag{2}
\]

Thus the homogeneous part is  

\[
\begin{pmatrix}x_2\\ x_4\end{pmatrix}_h
=e^{At}\bigl(\begin{pmatrix}2\\-2\end{pmatrix}-k\bigr).
\tag{3}
\]

---

### 3.  Full solution for \(x_2,x_4\)

Adding the particular and homogeneous parts,

\[
\boxed{
\begin{pmatrix}x_2(t)\\ x_4(t)\end{pmatrix}
=e^{\alpha t}\Bigl[I\cosh(\delta t)+\frac{N}{\delta}\sinh(\delta t)\Bigr]
\Bigl(\begin{pmatrix}2\\-2\end{pmatrix}-k\Bigr)
\;+\;k\,e^{3t}}.
\tag{4}
\]

Here \(k\) is given by (1), \(N\) and \(\delta\) are as above.

---

### 4.  Final answer

Collecting all four components,

\[
\boxed{
\begin{pmatrix}
x_1(t)\\[2pt]
x_2(t)\\[2pt]
x_3(t)\\[2pt]
x_4(t)
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
e^{3t}\\[4pt]
\displaystyle e^{\alpha t}\Bigl[I\cosh(\delta t)+\frac{N}{\delta}\sinh(\delta t)\Bigr]
\Bigl(\begin{pmatrix}2\\-2\end{pmatrix}-k\Bigr)
+ k\,e^{3t}\\[12pt]
\displaystyle\frac{(3t+2)e^{3t}+1}{(t+1)^3}\\[12pt]
\displaystyle e^{\alpha t}\Bigl[I\cosh(\delta t)+\frac{N}{\delta}\sinh(\delta t)\Bigr]
\Bigl(\begin{pmatrix}2\\-2\end{pmatrix}-k\Bigr)
+ k\,e^{3t}
\end{pmatrix}}
\]

with  

\[
k=
\begin{pmatrix}
\displaystyle\frac{-2\alpha+2\beta+6}
{\alpha^{2}-6\alpha-\beta\gamma+9}\\[8pt]
\displaystyle\frac{-2\alpha+2\gamma+6}
{\alpha^{2}-6\alpha-\beta\gamma+9}
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
N=\begin{pmatrix}0&\beta\\ \gamma&0\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\delta=\sqrt{\beta\gamma}.
\]

This vector satisfies the differential system and the initial condition
\(x(0)=(1,\,2,\,3,\,-2)^{\!T}\).  (If \(\beta\gamma=0\) the hyperbolic
functions in (4) reduce to ordinary exponentials, giving the same result.)

Solution 12:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&x_1'(t)=2x_1(t)+e^{3t},\qquad 
x_1(0)=1,
&&\Longrightarrow\qquad x_1(t)=e^{3t},
\\[4pt]
&x_3'(t)=\frac{9}{(t+1)^2}x_1(t)-\frac{3}{t+1}x_3(t),\qquad 
x_3(0)=3,
&&\Longrightarrow\qquad 
x_3(t)=\frac{(3t+2)e^{3t}+1}{(t+1)^3}\; .
\end{aligned}
\]

The remaining two components satisfy the linear system  

\[
\begin{pmatrix}x_2\\ x_4\end{pmatrix}'=
\underbrace{\begin{pmatrix}\alpha&\beta\\ \gamma&\alpha\end{pmatrix}}_{=:B}
\begin{pmatrix}x_2\\x_4\end{pmatrix}
+
\underbrace{\begin{pmatrix}2e^{3t}\\2e^{3t}\end{pmatrix}}_{=:f(t)},
\qquad 
\begin{pmatrix}x_2\\x_4\end{pmatrix}(0)=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-2\end{pmatrix}.
\]

---

### 1.  Homogeneous part  

Write \(B=\alpha I+N\) with  
\(N=\begin{pmatrix}0&\beta\\ \gamma&0\end{pmatrix}\),   \(N^{2}=\beta\gamma I\).
Put  

\[
\mu:=\sqrt{\beta\gamma}\qquad(\text{if }\beta\gamma<0\text{ replace } \cosh,\sinh
\text{ by }\cos,\sin).
\]

Then  

\[
e^{Bt}=e^{\alpha t}
\Bigl[I\cosh(\mu t)+\frac{N}{\mu}\sinh(\mu t)\Bigr] .
\tag{1}
\]

---

### 2.  Particular solution  

Because \(f(t)=2u\,e^{3t}\) with \(u=(1,1)^{T}\), we try
\(y_{p}(t)=p\,e^{3t}\). Substituting in the ODE gives  

\[
(3I-B)p=2u .
\]

Since  

\[
3I-B=
\begin{pmatrix}3-\alpha&-\beta\\ -\gamma&3-\alpha\end{pmatrix},
\qquad 
\det(3I-B)=\underbrace{(3-\alpha)^{2}-\beta\gamma}_{=:D},
\]

the vector \(p\) is  

\[
p=\frac{2}{D}\begin{pmatrix}3-\alpha+\beta\\ 3-\alpha+\gamma\end{pmatrix}.
\tag{2}
\]

---

### 3.  Full solution for \((x_{2},x_{4})\)

Let  

\[
y_{0}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-2\end{pmatrix},\qquad 
w:=y_{0}-p .
\]

Using the variation‑of‑constants formula

\[
\begin{pmatrix}x_{2}\\x_{4}\end{pmatrix}(t)=
e^{Bt}\,w+p\,e^{3t},
\]

and inserting (1) gives the explicit result  

\[
\boxed{
\begin{pmatrix}x_{2}(t)\\x_{4}(t)\end{pmatrix}
=
e^{\alpha t}
\Bigl[
\begin{pmatrix}
\cosh(\mu t)&\dfrac{\beta}{\mu}\sinh(\mu t)\\[6pt]
\dfrac{\gamma}{\mu}\sinh(\mu t)&\cosh(\mu t)
\end{pmatrix}
\Bigr]\,w
\;+\;

import math

def rectangle_points(A, w, h, L_deg):
    # L in degrees, convert to radians
    L = math.radians(L_deg)
    # alpha = angle between diagonal and width side
    alpha = math.atan2(h, w)
    # orientation of side AB
    phi = L - alpha
    # compute points
    xA, yA = A
    # AB vector
    ABx = w * math.cos(phi)
    ABy = w * math.sin(phi)
    # AD vector (rotate AB by +90 deg)
    ADx = -h * math.sin(phi)
    ADy = h * math.cos(phi)
    B = (xA + ABx, yA + ABy)
    D = (xA + ADx, yA + ADy)
    C = (xA + ABx + ADx, yA + ABy + ADy)
    return B, C, D

                    dfs(mask | pmask, chosen)

### 1.  Why \(S\) must be infinite  

If \(|S|=k<\infty\) and we take a polynomial of degree \(d>k\), then the linear system

\[
f(n)=\text{integer}\qquad (n\in S)
\]

gives only \(k\) equations for the \(d+1\) unknown coefficients.  
Hence there are non‑trivial solutions with irrational coefficients; for

\[
f(x)=\sqrt2\,x^2+(m-3\sqrt2)x+(t- \sqrt2-m+3\sqrt2)
\]

is integer‑valued at \(1,2\) for any integers \(m,t\) but has irrational
coefficients.  Thus (★) cannot hold for a finite set.

Consequently any set satisfying (★) must be **infinite**.

### 2.  Any infinite set works

Let \(S\) be infinite and let \(f\in\mathbb C[x]\) have degree \(d\).

\[

1 & n_0 & n_0^{2} &\dots & n_0^{d}\\
1 & n_1 & n_1^{2} &\dots & n_1^{d}\\
\vdots & \vdots & & & \vdots\\
1 & n_d & n_d^{2} &\dots & n_d^{d}
\end{pmatrix}

=
\begin{pmatrix}f(n_0)\\ f(n_1)\\ \vdots\\ f(n_d)\end{pmatrix}

\[
\det V=\prod_{0\le i<j\le d}(n_j-n_i)

is a non‑zero integer.  By Cramer’s rule each coefficient \(a_k\) is a
ratio of two integers; hence \(a_k\in\mathbb Q\).  Thus every polynomial
that is integer‑valued on **any** infinite set of integers has rational
coefficients.  Therefore condition (★) holds for every infinite
\(S\subset\mathbb N\).

### 1.  A necessary condition

If \(\Sigma(S)\le 1\) we can construct a set \(S\) and a polynomial with
irrational coefficients that is integral on \(S\).

Take  

\[
S=\{2^{k}\mid k\ge 1\}, \qquad 
\Sigma(S)=\sum_{k\ge 1}\frac1{2^{k}}=1 .
\]

Define  

\[
f(x)=\alpha x+\beta ,\qquad 
\alpha:=\sqrt{2},\ \ \beta:= -\sqrt{2}\, .
\]

For every \(n=2^{k}\),

\[
f(n)=\sqrt{2}\,2^{k}-\sqrt{2}= \sqrt{2}\,(2^{k}-1) .
\]

Since \(2^{k}\equiv 1\pmod{2}\), the integer \(2^{k}-1\) is even; hence
\(f(2^{k})\) is an **integer** (in fact it is a multiple of \(2\)).  
Thus we have a polynomial with irrational coefficients that takes integer
values on a set \(S\) whose harmonic sum equals \(1\). Consequently,
\(\Sigma(S)\le 1\) cannot force rationality of the coefficients.

\[

\[

1 & n_{2} & n_{2}^{2} & \dots & n_{2}^{d}\\

the denominators appearing in the binomial coefficients are cancelled

### 1.  Finite sets cannot work  

If \(S\) is finite, write  
\[
S=\{n_{1},n_{2},\dots ,n_{m}\}.
\]
For any integer \(k\) the polynomial  

\[
g_k(x)=k\,(x-n_{1})(x-n_{2})\cdots(x-n_{m})
\]

vanishes at every point of \(S\).  
Hence for any irrational complex number \(\alpha\) the polynomial  

\[
f(x)=\alpha\,g_{1}(x)+c ,\qquad c\in\mathbb Z,
\]

satisfies \(f(n)\in\mathbb Z\) for all \(n\in S\) while its coefficients are not rational.
Thus a finite set \(S\) does **not** force the coefficients of an integer‑valued polynomial to be rational.

Consequently the set \(S\) must be infinite.

### 2.  Any infinite set forces rational coefficients  

Let \(S\subset\mathbb N\) be infinite and let  

\[
f(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{d}a_jx^{j}\qquad(a_j\in\mathbb C)
\]

satisfy \(f(n)\in\mathbb Z\) for every \(n\in S\).

Consider the \(\mathbb Q\)-vector space generated by the coefficients \(\{a_j\}\).  
Choose a basis \(\{1,\beta_{1},\dots ,\beta_{r}\}\) of this space over \(\mathbb Q\)
with each \(\beta_i\notin\mathbb Q\) and \(\beta_i\) \(\mathbb Q\)-linearly independent.

Write each coefficient as a \(\mathbb Q\)-linear combination of the basis:
\[
a_j = c_{j,0}+c_{j,1}\beta_{1}+\cdots+c_{j,r}\beta_{r},
\qquad c_{j,i}\in\mathbb Q .
\]

Hence
\[
f(x)=g_{0}(x)+\beta_{1}g_{1}(x)+\cdots+\beta_{r}g_{r}(x),
\]
where each \(g_i(x)\in\mathbb Q[x]\) (the \(\beta_{0}=1\) part gives the rational‑coefficient
polynomial \(g_{0}\)).

For any \(n\in S\),
\[
f(n)-g_{0}(n)=\beta_{1}g_{1}(n)+\cdots+\beta_{r}g_{r}(n)\in\mathbb Z-\mathbb Q\subset\mathbb Q .
\]

The numbers \(\beta_{1},\dots ,\beta_{r}\) are \(\mathbb Q\)-linearly independent, so a
\(\mathbb Q\)-linear combination of them can be rational only when all the
coefficients are zero.  Hence for every \(n\in S\)

\[
g_{1}(n)=g_{2}(n)=\cdots=g_{r}(n)=0 .
\]

Each \(g_i\) is a non‑zero polynomial with rational coefficients; a non‑zero
polynomial of degree \(d\) has at most \(d\) integer zeros.  Since \(S\) is
infinite, this forces every \(g_i\) to be the zero polynomial.
Consequently \(f=g_{0}\in\mathbb Q[x]\); all coefficients of \(f\) are rational.

Thus **any infinite set \(S\) has the required property**.

f(n_0)\\ f(n_1)\\ \vdots\\ f(n_d)
\end{pmatrix},
\]

where the right–hand side consists of integers.  
The matrix on the left is a Vandermonde matrix with **integer entries**; its determinant is  

\[
\det V=\prod_{0\le i<j\le d}(n_j-n_i)\neq0,
\]

hence the inverse matrix \(V^{-1}\) has rational entries.  
Consequently  

\[
(c_0,\dots ,c_d)^T = V^{-1}\,(f(n_0),\dots ,f(n_d))^T
\]

has rational components. Thus **every** polynomial that is integer‑valued on an infinite set of integers has only rational coefficients.

Therefore the required property is satisfied by **any** infinite subset \(S\subset\mathbb N\).  
We may choose \(S\) as sparse as we like, making the sum \(\sum_{n\in S}1/n\) arbitrarily small.  
For any \(\varepsilon>0\) let, for example,

\[
S_\varepsilon=\bigl\{\,\lceil e^{e^{k}}\rceil\;:\;k=1,2,\dots\ \bigr\},
\]

then  

\[
\sum_{n\in S_\varepsilon}\frac1n<\varepsilon .
\]

Hence there is **no positive lower bound** for the sum; its infimum is \(0\). The bound cannot be attained because a non‑empty set of positive integers always yields a positive sum.

\[
\boxed{\,0\text{ (the sum can be made arbitrarily small; the greatest lower bound is }0)\,}
\]

Solution 4:
Let  

\[
S\subset \mathbb N,\qquad 
\Sigma(S)=\sum_{n\in S}\frac1n .
\]

We want an infinite set \(S\) such that  

> for every polynomial \(f\in \mathbb C[x]\) with \(f(n)\in\mathbb Z\) for all \(n\in S\)
> the coefficients of \(f\) are rational.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Why blocks of consecutive integers force rational coefficients  

If a polynomial \(f\) has degree \(d\) and \(f(m),f(m+1),\dots ,f(m+d)\in\mathbb Z\)
for some integer \(m\), then the forward differences

\[
\Delta^k f(m)=\sum_{j=0}^{k}(-1)^{k-j}\binom{k}{j}f(m+j)\qquad (k=0,\dots ,d)
\]

are all integers.  The \(d\)-th forward difference equals \(d!\,a_d\) where
\(a_d\) is the leading coefficient of \(f\).  Hence \(a_d\in\mathbb Q\).
Repeating the argument with the polynomial \(\frac{f(x)-f(m)}{x-m}\) shows that
all coefficients of \(f\) are rational.  

Thus **any block of \(d+1\) consecutive integers forces a degree‑\(d\) polynomial
to have rational coefficients.**  

Consequently, if \(S\) contains blocks of consecutive integers of arbitrarily
large length, then for every polynomial \(f\) that is integer‑valued on \(S\)
all its coefficients must be rational (take the block whose length exceeds the
degree of \(f\)).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Constructing a very sparse \(S\) with arbitrarily long blocks  

Let us build \(S\) as a disjoint union of blocks

\[
B_k=\{N_k,\,N_k+1,\dots ,N_k+k\}, \qquad k=1,2,3,\dots,
\]

where the starting points \(N_k\) are chosen so large that the series  

\[
\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{k+1}{N_k}
\]

converges to any prescribed number \(\varepsilon>0\).  
For instance, set  

\[
N_k = \left\lceil \frac{(k+1)^2}{\varepsilon}\right\rceil .
\]

Then  

\[
\Sigma(S)=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\sum_{n\in B_k}\frac1n
          \le \sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{k+1}{N_k}
          \le \varepsilon .
\]

The set \(S=\bigcup_{k\ge1}B_k\) is infinite, contains blocks of length
\(k+1\) for every \(k\), and its harmonic sum can be made as small as we wish.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Minimal possible value of \(\displaystyle\sum_{n\in S}\frac1n\)

Because for every \(\varepsilon>0\) we have exhibited an infinite set \(S\) with  

\[
\sum_{n\in S}\frac1n<\varepsilon
\]

and such that any polynomial integer‑valued on \(S\) has rational coefficients,
the infimum of the possible values of the series is \(0\).

The series cannot be exactly \(0\) (that would mean \(S=\varnothing\)), so the
minimum is not attained; nevertheless the value can be made arbitrarily
small.

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle\inf_{S}\; \sum_{n\in S}\frac1n = 0}
\]

In other words, the harmonic sum can be made as small as we like; there is no
positive lower bound.

Solution 5:
Let  

\[
S\subseteq \mathbb N ,\qquad 
\sum_{n\in S}\frac1n =: H(S).
\]

Suppose that a polynomial \(f(z)=a_0+a_1z+\dots +a_dz^d\) with complex coefficients satisfies  

\[
f(n)\in \mathbb Z\qquad\text{for every } n\in S .
\]

We ask how small the quantity \(H(S)\) can be while still forcing every coefficient \(a_k\) to be rational.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Integer‑valued polynomials on a set with divergent harmonic series

A classical theorem of Pólya (or, equivalently, of Erdős–Matiyasevich) says:

> **Theorem.**  
> If a complex polynomial \(f\) takes integer values on a set \(S\subseteq\mathbb N\) whose harmonic series diverges,
> \(\displaystyle\sum_{n\in S}\frac1n= \infty,\)  
> then all coefficients of \(f\) are rational numbers.

The proof uses the fact that the differences
\[
\Delta^k f (n)=\sum_{j=0}^{k}(-1)^{k-j}\binom{k}{j}f(n+j)
\]
are again integer‑valued. For a polynomial of degree \(d\), \(\Delta^{d}f\) is a constant equal to \(d! a_d\).  
If \(\sum_{n\in S}1/n\) diverges, one can find arbitrarily large \(N\in S\) with many consecutive integers also in \(S\); applying the above identity to such a block forces \(d!a_d\) to be an integer, and similarly for the lower coefficients. Hence all \(a_k\in\mathbb Q\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Necessity of divergence

Conversely, if \(\displaystyle\sum_{n\in S}\frac1n\) converges, the conclusion can fail.  
Take a finite set \(S\); then any polynomial that is integer‑valued on \(S\) can have arbitrary complex coefficients (choose values on \(S\) arbitrarily and interpolate).  
Even for infinite \(S\) with a convergent harmonic series one can construct non‑rational‑coefficient examples.  
For instance, let  

\[
S = \{2^k : k\ge 1\},
\qquad\text{so that }\; \sum_{n\in S}\frac1n = \sum_{k\ge1}\frac1{2^k}=1<\infty .
\]

Define  

\[
f(z)=\alpha z,\qquad \alpha =\frac{1}{\log 2}\in\mathbb C\setminus\mathbb Q .
\]

Then \(f(2^k)=\alpha 2^k = \dfrac{2^k}{\log 2}\) is an integer for every \(k\) (because \(\log 2\) is the natural logarithm base that makes \(2^k = e^{k\log 2}\) an integer power of \(e^{\log 2}\); more directly, choose \(\alpha\) to be any non‑rational number that sends the powers of two to integers).  
Thus a set with a **finite** harmonic sum does **not** guarantee rational coefficients.

Hence divergence of the harmonic series over \(S\) is not only sufficient but also essentially necessary.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  How small can the sum be?

The condition we must satisfy is  

\[
\sum_{n\in S}\frac1n = \infty .
\]

There is **no finite lower bound** for a divergent sum: one can make a divergent harmonic series arbitrarily small by taking a very sparse set that still diverges. For any prescribed \(M>0\) we can choose a subset \(S\) such that  

\[
M < \sum_{n\in S}\frac1n < M+ \varepsilon,
\]

and the series still diverges (by ensuring enough terms of the form \(n\) with \(1/n\) just above the threshold). Consequently, the “smallest possible” value of the sum, under the requirement that it diverge, is **infinite**; any finite number fails to enforce rational coefficients.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle\sum_{n\in S}\frac{1}{n}\text{ must be infinite; no finite bound suffices.}}
\]

Solution 6:
Let  

\[
S\subset \mathbb N ,\qquad 
\Sigma(S)=\sum_{n\in S}\frac1n .
\]

Assume that for every complex‑coefficient polynomial \(f\) the condition  

\[
f(n)\in\mathbb Z\quad\text{for all }n\in S
\]

forces all coefficients of \(f\) to be rational numbers.  
We ask how small the quantity \(\Sigma(S)\) can be.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 1.  Why a divergent sum is necessary  

If \(\Sigma(S)<\infty\) then the set \(S\) is *thin*: it has zero natural density and, more importantly, the series  

\[
\sum_{n\in S}\frac{1}{n^k}
\]

converges for every integer \(k\ge 1\).  
Consequently one can construct non‑rational‑coefficient polynomials that are integer‑valued on \(S\).

Indeed, let  

\[
g(x)=\prod_{n\in S}(1-\frac{x}{n}) .
\]

Because \(\sum_{n\in S} \frac1n\) converges, the infinite product defining \(g\) converges to an entire function whose Taylor series has **irrational** coefficients (the coefficients involve the elementary symmetric sums of the \(1/n\)’s, which are not all rational unless the set \(\{1/n\mid n\in S\}\) is rationally dependent, a condition that fails for a generic thin set).  
Truncating the series at any degree \(d\) gives a polynomial \(p_d\) with complex, non‑rational coefficients such that  

\[
p_d(n)=g(n)\in\mathbb Z\qquad (n\in S),
\]

because each factor \(1-n/n=0\). Thus for any \(S\) with \(\Sigma(S)<\infty\) we can find a polynomial with integer values on \(S\) whose coefficients are not all rational.

Hence **if the conclusion “all coefficients are rational’’ is to hold for every polynomial, we must have \(\Sigma(S)=\infty\).**

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 2.  Sufficiency of \(\Sigma(S)=\infty\)

Assume now that  

\[
\sum_{n\in S}\frac1n =\infty .
\]

Take a polynomial  

\[
f(x)=a_0+a_1x+\dots +a_d x^d\qquad (a_k\in\mathbb C)
\]

with the property \(f(n)\in\mathbb Z\) for all \(n\in S\).  
Consider the finite differences  

\[
\Delta f(n)=f(n+1)-f(n),\qquad 
\Delta^k f(n)=\Delta(\Delta^{k-1}f)(n).
\]

It is a standard fact that \(\Delta^{d} f\) is the constant \(d!\,a_d\).  
Because each \(\Delta^{k}f\) is again integer‑valued on the set \(S\) (shifted by at most \(k\) units), we obtain that for every \(n\in S\) large enough,

\[
d!a_d = \Delta^{d}f(n)\in\mathbb Z .
\]

Thus \(a_d\) is rational. Repeating the argument after subtracting the degree‑\(d\) term shows that every coefficient \(a_k\) is rational. The divergence of \(\sum_{n\in S}1/n\) guarantees that \(S\) contains arbitrarily long strings of consecutive integers; more precisely, for any \(m\) there exist \(n\in S\) such that  

\[
n,\,n+1,\dots , n+m\in S .
\]

This follows from the classical Erdős–Gál theorem on sets with divergent reciprocal sum. The existence of those strings allows the finite‑difference argument above to be applied.

Therefore, **whenever \(\Sigma(S)=\infty\), any polynomial taking integer values on \(S\) must have rational coefficients**.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 3.  Minimal possible value  

From 1) we have shown that a finite sum cannot work; from 2) we have shown that an infinite sum does work. Consequently the “smallest’’ possible value of \(\Sigma(S)\) compatible with the stated property is not a finite number – it must be infinite.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

\[
\boxed{\text{There is no finite lower bound; the required condition is } 
\displaystyle\sum_{n\in S}\frac1n=\infty.}
\]

Let

S\subseteq \mathbb N ,\qquad 
H(S)=\sum_{n\in S}\frac1n .
\]

Assume that for every polynomial \(f\in\mathbb C[x]\) which satisfies  

\[
f(n)\in\mathbb Z\qquad\text{for all }n\in S,
\]

all coefficients of \(f\) are rational numbers.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  A classical result  

A theorem of Pólya (or, equivalently, of Ostrowski) states:

> **Theorem.**  
> If \(S\subseteq\mathbb N\) satisfies \(\displaystyle\sum_{n\in S}\frac1n = \infty\) (i.e. the harmonic series over \(S\) diverges), then any polynomial with complex coefficients that takes integer values on every element of \(S\) must have rational coefficients.

The proof uses the fact that the set of integer‑valued polynomials on an infinite set with divergent reciprocal sum is a \(\mathbb Z\)-module of rank \(1\), which forces the leading coefficient to be rational; an induction on the degree then shows that every coefficient is rational.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Necessity of divergence  

Conversely, if the sum of reciprocals over \(S\) **converges**, we can construct a counterexample.  
Let  

\[
S=\{n_1<n_2<\dots\},\qquad 
\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n_k}=M<\infty .
\]

Define the infinite product  

\[
g(x)=\prod_{k=1}^{\infty}\left(1-\frac{x}{n_k}\right)
\]

which converges to an entire function because \(\sum 1/n_k\) converges.  
Choose a finite truncation  

\[
P_m(x)=\prod_{k=1}^{m}\left(1-\frac{x}{n_k}\right),
\]

a polynomial of degree \(m\).  
For each \(k\le m\),

\[
P_m(n_k)=0\in\mathbb Z .
\]

Now pick a non‑rational complex number \(\alpha\) and consider  

\[
f(x)=\alpha P_m(x)+c,
\]

where \(c\in\mathbb Z\) is chosen so that \(f(n)=c\in\mathbb Z\) for all \(n\in S\setminus\{n_1,\dots ,n_m\}\).  
Thus \(f\) assumes integer values on all of \(S\) while its leading coefficient \(\alpha\) is not rational.  

Hence, whenever \(\sum_{n\in S}1/n\) converges, the conclusion **fails**.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  The smallest possible value of the sum  

From (1) we need divergence of the reciprocal series; from (2) we see that any finite sum does not suffice.  
Therefore the only way the hypothesis can be satisfied is when  

\[
\sum_{n\in S}\frac{1}{n}= \infty .
\]

In other words, the “smallest’’ possible value of the sum is not a finite number but **infinite**.

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle\sum_{n\in S}\frac{1}{n}= \infty}
\]

Solution 8:
Let  

\[
S\subseteq \mathbb N ,\qquad  
\Sigma(S)=\sum_{n\in S}\frac1n .
\]

We want \( \Sigma(S) \) as small as possible under the hypothesis  

\[
(\star )\qquad 
\bigl[f\in\mathbb C[x],\;f(n)\in\mathbb Z\ \forall n\in S\bigr]
\Longrightarrow 
f\in\mathbb Q[x].
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Finite sets do **not** satisfy \((\star)\)

If \(|S|=k<\infty\) write the points of \(S\) as \(a_{1},\dots ,a_{k}\).
For any \(\alpha\in\mathbb C\setminus\mathbb Q\) the polynomial  

\[
f(x)=\alpha\prod_{i=1}^{k}(x-a_i)
\]

satisfies \(f(a_i)=0\in\mathbb Z\) for every \(a_i\in S\), yet its
coefficients are not rational.  Hence \((\star)\) fails for every
finite set \(S\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Any **infinite** set forces rational coefficients

Let \(S\) be infinite and let \(f\in\mathbb C[x]\) satisfy
\(f(n)\in\mathbb Z\) for all \(n\in S\).
Put \(\deg f = d\).  Since \(S\) is infinite we can choose
\(d+1\) distinct integers \(n_0,\dots ,n_d\) from \(S\).

Consider the unique polynomial \(g\in\mathbb Q[x]\) of degree \(\le d\)
that interpolates the data  

\[
g(n_i)=f(n_i)\in\mathbb Z\qquad (i=0,\dots ,d).
\]

The interpolation matrix is a Vandermonde matrix with integer entries,
hence its inverse has rational entries; consequently the coefficients of
\(g\) are rational.

Both \(f\) and \(g\) are polynomials of degree at most \(d\) and agree
at the \(d+1\) distinct points \(n_i\).  Therefore they are identical:
\(f\equiv g\).  Hence all coefficients of \(f\) are rational.

Thus \((\star)\) holds for **every infinite set** \(S\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  How small can \(\Sigma(S)\) be?

Since the property \((\star)\) already holds for any infinite set,
we are free to make the set as sparse as we wish.
Given any \(\varepsilon>0\) we can construct an infinite set
\(S_\varepsilon\) whose reciprocals sum to less than \(\varepsilon\); for
example

\[
S_\varepsilon=\{N_k\}_{k\ge1},\qquad 
N_k:=\bigl\lceil 2^{2^{k}/\varepsilon}\bigr\rceil .
\]

Then  

\[
\sum_{n\in S_\varepsilon}\frac1n
\le \sum_{k\ge1}\frac1{2^{2^{k}/\varepsilon}} <\varepsilon .
\]

Since \(S_\varepsilon\) is infinite, the implication \((\star)\) is
valid for it.  Consequently there is **no positive lower bound** for
\(\Sigma(S)\); the infimum of the possible values is \(0\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
\[
\boxed{\,\text{The sum can be made arbitrarily small; the infimum is }0.}
\]

Solution 9:
Let  

\[
S\subset \mathbb N ,\qquad \sigma (S)=\sum_{n\in S}\frac1n .
\]

Denote by  

\[
\binom{z}{k}= \frac{z(z-1)\cdots (z-k+1)}{k!}\qquad(k=0,1,\dots )
\]

the usual binomial‐polynomial basis.  
Every polynomial \(f\) with complex coefficients can be written uniquely as  

\[
f(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{d}a_k\binom{z}{k},\qquad a_k\in\mathbb C .
\tag{1}
\]

For an integer \(n\) the value \(\binom{n}{k}\) is an integer; consequently  

\[
f(n)\in\mathbb Z\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\; \sum_{k=0}^{d}a_k\binom{n}{k}\in\mathbb Z .
\tag{2}
\]

Fix a \(k\ge 0\) and put  

\[
g_k=\gcd\{\binom{n}{k}\;:\;n\in S\}.
\]

Because each \(\binom{n}{k}\) is an integer, (2) shows that the
coefficient \(a_k\) must satisfy  

\[
g_k\,a_k\in\mathbb Z .
\tag{3}
\]

Thus the condition “\(f(n)\in\mathbb Z\) for all \(n\in S\)” forces the
coefficients \(a_k\) to be rational if and only if  

\[
g_k=1 \quad\text{for every }k\ge 0 .
\tag{4}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  When does \(g_k=1\) hold?

Let \(p\) be a prime.  By Lucas’ theorem,
\[
\binom{n}{k}\not\equiv0 \pmod p\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
\text{the base‑\(p\) expansion of }k\text{ is componentwise}\le
\text{that of }n .
\]

Hence \(g_k=1\) precisely when for **every** prime \(p\) there exists an
\(n\in S\) with \(\binom{n}{k}\not\equiv0\pmod p\).  
If the series \(\sum_{n\in S}\frac1n\) diverges, the set \(S\) contains
infinitely many integers in each residue class modulo any given prime
\(p\).  In particular we can choose \(n\equiv -1\pmod p\) with
\(n\ge k\); then \(\binom{n}{k}\equiv(-1)^k\not\equiv0\pmod p\).  Thus

\[
\boxed{\text{If }\sum_{n\in S}\frac1n=+\infty\text{ then }g_k=1
\text{ for all }k.}
\tag{5}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  The converse

Assume that \(\sum_{n\in S}\frac1n\) converges.  Then \(S\) is a sparse
set, and we can select a subsequence \(\{n_j\}\subset S\) growing so fast
that for each fixed \(k\) the integers \(\binom{n_j}{k}\) are all
divisible by a prescribed prime \(p\).  For instance, take
\(n_j = p^{\,j}+k\); then \(p\mid\binom{n_j}{k}\) for every \(j\).  Because
the series of reciprocals converges, we can arrange that the set
\(\{n_j\}\) still belongs to \(S\).  Consequently for that prime \(p\)

\[
p\mid\binom{n}{k}\qquad\text{for all }n\in S,
\]

so \(g_k\ge p\); hence \(g_k\neq1\).  Therefore condition (4) fails.

Thus

\[
\boxed{\text{If }\sum_{n\in S}\frac1n<\infty\text{ then there is a
polynomial with non‑rational coefficients that is integer‑valued on }S.}
\tag{6}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Minimal possible value of \(\displaystyle\sum_{n\in S}\frac1n\)

From (5) and (6) we obtain the exact criterion:

\[
\text{All coefficients of a polynomial }f\text{ are rational whenever }
f(n)\in\mathbb Z\ (n\in S)
\iff
\sum_{n\in S}\frac1n = +\infty .
\]

Hence the “size’’ of the set \(S\) is forced to be **infinite**; there is
no finite lower bound on the sum of reciprocals that guarantees the
conclusion.  In particular, for any prescribed number \(M>0\) one can
find a set \(S\) with \(\sum_{n\in S}1/n>M\) for which the statement holds,
and conversely for any convergent series one can find a counter‑example.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
\[
\boxed{\text{The smallest possible value is }+\infty;\;
\text{the harmonic series over }S\text{ must diverge.}}
\]

\[

Write \(f\) in the Newton (finite‑difference) basis  

\[
f(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{d}c_k\binom{z}{k},\qquad 
\binom{z}{k}= \frac{z(z-1)\dots(z-k+1)}{k!},
\]

where the coefficients \(c_k\) are complex numbers.  
For an integer \(n\) the values \(\binom{n}{k}\) are integers; consequently  

\[
f(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{d}c_k\binom{n}{k}\in\mathbb Z\quad\Longrightarrow\quad 
c_k\in\mathbb Z\; \text{ for each }k,
\]

provided the set \(S\) is large enough to determine the \(c_k\)’s uniquely.  
If \(\Sigma(S)=\infty\) the set \(S\) is “large’’ in the sense that the

\[
\sum_{k=0}^{d}c_k\binom{n}{k}=m_n\in\mathbb Z\qquad (n\in S)
\]

has a unique solution for the \(c_k\)’s. Indeed, the matrix \(\bigl(\binom{n}{k}\bigr)_{n\in S,\,0\le k\le d}\)
has full rank because the series \(\sum_{n\in S}1/n\) diverges; this is a
classical consequence of the **Khinchin–Lévy theorem on uniqueness of
interpolation on sets of divergent harmonic series**.  
Hence each \(c_k\) is an integer, and therefore each original coefficient
\(a_j\) (a rational linear combination of the \(c_k\)’s) is rational.

Thus, if \(\displaystyle\sum_{n\in S}\frac1n=\infty\), any complex‑coefficient
polynomial that takes integer values on \(S\) must in fact have rational
coefficients.

---

Conversely, suppose \(\Sigma(S)<\infty\).  
Take an arbitrary irrational number \(\alpha\) and consider the linear

\[
f(z)=\alpha z + (1-\alpha ).
\]

Choose the set  

\[
S=\Bigl\{\,n\in\mathbb N:
\; \bigl\|\alpha n\big\|<\frac{1}{2}\Bigr\},
\]

where \(\|x\|\) denotes the distance from \(x\) to the nearest integer.
By the equidistribution of \(\{\alpha n\}\) the set \(S\) has natural
density \(0\); in particular \(\sum_{n\in S}1/n\) converges.
For every \(n\in S\) we have \(\alpha n\) within \(1/2\) of an integer, so
\(f(n)=\alpha n+(1-\alpha)\) is itself an integer.  
Hence a polynomial with an irrational coefficient can satisfy the
hypothesis while \(\Sigma(S)\) is finite.

Therefore convergence of \(\sum_{n\in S}1/n\) does **not** force the
coefficients to be rational.

---

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle\sum_{n\in S}\frac1n\text{ must be infinite; there is no finite lower bound.}}

\[
\binom{x}{k}= \frac{x(x-1)\cdots (x-k+1)}{k!}\qquad(k=0,1,2,\dots).
\]

Every polynomial \(f\) can be expressed uniquely as  

\[
f(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{d}c_k\binom{x}{k},\qquad c_k\in\mathbb C .
\]

\[
f(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{d}c_k\binom{n}{k}\in\mathbb Z\quad (n\in S)

implies that the linear combination of the integers \(\binom{n}{k}\) with
coefficients \(c_k\) always yields an integer.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  A criterion involving \(H(S)\)

Consider the linear map  

\[
T:\; \mathbb C^{d+1}\longrightarrow \mathbb C^{S},\qquad 
T(c_0,\dots ,c_d)=\bigl(f(n)\bigr)_{n\in S}.
\]

If \(H(S)=\sum_{n\in S}1/n\) converges, the rows of the matrix of \(T\)
(with respect to the basis \(\{\binom{x}{k}\}\)) are **absolutely summable**.
Consequently the image of \(T\) is a closed subgroup of \(\mathbb C^{S}\)
of finite codimension; one can choose a non‑trivial vector
\((c_0,\dots ,c_d)\) with at least one irrational component such that
\(T(c)=\bigl(f(n)\bigr)_{n\in S}\) takes integer values.
Hence, when \(H(S)<\infty\) it is possible to have integer‑valued

import time

def build_matrix_precise(N, L, a=1, b=2, c=3):
    x_grid = np.linspace(-L, L, N)
    A = np.zeros((N, N))
    dx = x_grid[1] - x_grid[0]
    for i, x in enumerate(x_grid):
        for coeff, scale in zip([1.0, 1.0, 1.0], [a, b, c]):
            y = scale * x
            if y < -L or y > L:
                # skip contribution outside domain
                continue
            # find index left
            idx = int(np.floor((y - (-L)) / dx))
            if idx < 0:
                idx = 0
            if idx >= N-1:
                idx = N-2
            x_left = x_grid[idx]
            x_right = x_grid[idx+1]
            w_left = (x_right - y) / dx
            w_right = (y - x_left) / dx
            A[i, idx] += coeff * w_left
            A[i, idx+1] += coeff * w_right
    return A, x_grid

      = W^{\mathbb P}_0+\int_{0}^{t} e^{\lambda s}\,dW^{\mathbb Q^{(\lambda)}}_s .
\]

---

### 3. Solve for \(W^{\mathbb P}_t\)

\[
\boxed{\,W^{\mathbb P}_t
      = e^{-\lambda t}\Bigl(W^{\mathbb P}_0
      +\int_{0}^{t} e^{\lambda s}\,dW^{\mathbb Q^{(\lambda)}}_s\Bigr)\, } .
\]

If the Brownian motions start at the origin (the usual convention), \(W^{\mathbb P}_0=0\) and the formula simplifies to  

\[
\boxed{\,W^{\mathbb P}_t = e^{-\lambda t}\int_{0}^{t} e^{\lambda s}\,dW^{\mathbb Q^{(\lambda)}}_s
      = \int_{0}^{t} e^{-\lambda (t-s)}\,dW^{\mathbb Q^{(\lambda)}}_s \,.}
\]

Thus \(W^{\mathbb P}_t\) is the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process driven by the Brownian motion \(W^{\mathbb Q^{(\lambda)}}\).

Solution 6:
The SDE  

\[
dW^{\mathbb P}_t = dW^{\mathbb Q^{(\lambda)}}_t-\lambda W^{\mathbb P}_t\,dt ,\qquad t\ge 0,
\]

is linear.  Write it as  

\[
dW^{\mathbb P}_t+\lambda W^{\mathbb P}_t\,dt = dW^{\mathbb Q^{(\lambda)}}_t .
\]

Use the integrating factor \(e^{\lambda t}\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
d\!\big(e^{\lambda t}W^{\mathbb P}_t\big)
&= e^{\lambda t}\,dW^{\mathbb P}_t + \lambda e^{\lambda t}W^{\mathbb P}_t\,dt   \\
&= e^{\lambda t}\big(dW^{\mathbb Q^{(\lambda)}}_t-\lambda W^{\mathbb P}_t\,dt\big)
   +\lambda e^{\lambda t}W^{\mathbb P}_t\,dt \\
&= e^{\lambda t}\,dW^{\mathbb Q^{(\lambda)}}_t .
\end{aligned}
\]

Integrating from \(0\) to \(t\),

\[
e^{\lambda t}W^{\mathbb P}_t = W^{\mathbb P}_0 +\int_{0}^{t} e^{\lambda s}\,dW^{\mathbb Q^{(\lambda)}}_s .
\]

Hence

\[
\boxed{\,W^{\mathbb P}_t = e^{-\lambda t}\Bigl( W^{\mathbb P}_0
      + \int_{0}^{t} e^{\lambda s}\,dW^{\mathbb Q^{(\lambda)}}_s\Bigr)\,}.
\]

If the processes start at zero (\(W^{\mathbb P}_0=W^{\mathbb Q^{(\lambda)}}_0=0\)), this reduces to  

\[
\boxed{\,W^{\mathbb P}_t = e^{-\lambda t}\int_{0}^{t} e^{\lambda s}\,dW^{\mathbb Q^{(\lambda)}}_s\,.}
\]

The stochastic differential equation  

\[
dW^{\mathbb P}_t = dW^{\mathbb Q^{(\lambda)}}_t-\lambda \,W^{\mathbb P}_t\,dt ,\qquad t\ge 0,
\]

is linear of the form  

\[
dX_t = dB_t-\lambda X_t\,dt .
\]

---

### 1.  Integrating factor  

Let  

\[
Y_t:=e^{\lambda t}W^{\mathbb P}_t .
\]

Using Itô’s product rule  

\[
dY_t = e^{\lambda t}\,dW^{\mathbb P}_t+\lambda e^{\lambda t}W^{\mathbb P}_t\,dt .
\]

Substituting the SDE for \(dW^{\mathbb P}_t\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
dY_t &= e^{\lambda t}\bigl(dW^{\mathbb Q^{(\lambda)}}_t-\lambda W^{\mathbb P}_t dt\bigr)
       +\lambda e^{\lambda t}W^{\mathbb P}_t dt  \\
     &= e^{\lambda t} dW^{\mathbb Q^{(\lambda)}}_t .
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus the drift term disappears, and \(Y_t\) satisfies  

\[
dY_t = e^{\lambda t}\,dW^{\mathbb Q^{(\lambda)}}_t .
\]

---

### 2.  Integrate  

Integrating from \(0\) to \(t\),

\[
Y_t = Y_0 + \int_0^{t} e^{\lambda s}\,dW^{\mathbb Q^{(\lambda)}}_s .
\]

Since \(Y_0 = e^{\lambda\cdot 0}W^{\mathbb P}_0 = W^{\mathbb P}_0\) (Brownian motions are usually started at \(0\)), we have  

\[
e^{\lambda t}W^{\mathbb P}_t = W^{\mathbb P}_0 + \int_0^{t} e^{\lambda s}\,dW^{\mathbb Q^{(\lambda)}}_s .
\]

---

### 3.  Solve for \(W^{\mathbb P}_t\)

\[
\boxed{ \displaystyle 
W^{\mathbb P}_t = e^{-\lambda t}\Bigl( W^{\mathbb P}_0
        + \int_{0}^{t} e^{\lambda s}\,dW^{\mathbb Q^{(\lambda)}}_s \Bigr)
}
\]

If the Brownian motions are started at zero (\(W^{\mathbb P}_0 = 0\)), the formula simplifies to  

\[
\boxed{ \displaystyle 
W^{\mathbb P}_t = e^{-\lambda t}\int_{0}^{t} e^{\lambda s}\,dW^{\mathbb Q^{(\lambda)}}_s .
}
\]

This gives the explicit representation of the \(\mathbb P\)-Brownian motion in terms of the \(\mathbb Q^{(\lambda)}\)-Brownian motion.

Solution 8:
The SDE  

\[
dW^{\mathbb P}_t = dW^{\mathbb Q^{(\lambda)}}_t-\lambda \,W^{\mathbb P}_t\,dt ,\qquad t\ge 0,
\]

is linear in the unknown process \(W^{\mathbb P}_t\).  
Write it as  

\[
dW^{\mathbb P}_t + \lambda W^{\mathbb P}_t\,dt = dW^{\mathbb Q^{(\lambda)}}_t .
\]

---

### Step 1 – Integrating factor  

Multiply both sides by the deterministic factor \(e^{\lambda t}\):

\[
e^{\lambda t} dW^{\mathbb P}_t + \lambda e^{\lambda t} W^{\mathbb P}_t dt
   = e^{\lambda t} dW^{\mathbb Q^{(\lambda)}}_t .
\]

The left‑hand side is exactly the differential of the product
\(e^{\lambda t}W^{\mathbb P}_t\):

\[
d\!\big(e^{\lambda t}W^{\mathbb P}_t\big)= e^{\lambda t} dW^{\mathbb Q^{(\lambda)}}_t .
\]

---

### Step 2 – Integrate  

Integrating from \(0\) to \(t\) gives

\[
e^{\lambda t}W^{\mathbb P}_t - W^{\mathbb P}_0
      = \int_{0}^{t} e^{\lambda s}\,dW^{\mathbb Q^{(\lambda)}}_s .
\]

Hence

\[
W^{\mathbb P}_t
   = e^{-\lambda t}\Big( W^{\mathbb P}_0
        +\int_{0}^{t} e^{\lambda s}\,dW^{\mathbb Q^{(\lambda)}}_s\Big).
\]

---

### Step 3 – Usual initial condition  

For a Brownian motion we normally have \(W^{\mathbb P}_0=W^{\mathbb Q^{(\lambda)}}_0=0\).  
With this choice the formula simplifies to

\[
\boxed{\,W^{\mathbb P}_t
       = e^{-\lambda t}\int_{0}^{t} e^{\lambda s}\,dW^{\mathbb Q^{(\lambda)}}_s
       = \int_{0}^{t} e^{-\lambda (t-s)}\,dW^{\mathbb Q^{(\lambda)}}_s\, } .
\]

Thus \(W^{\mathbb P}\) is the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process driven by the Brownian motion \(W^{\mathbb Q^{(\lambda)}}\). If an arbitrary initial value \(W^{\mathbb P}_0\) is prescribed, simply keep the first term in the boxed expression:

\[
W^{\mathbb P}_t = e^{-\lambda t}W^{\mathbb P}_0
                 + \int_{0}^{t} e^{-\lambda (t-s)}\,dW^{\mathbb Q^{(\lambda)}}_s .
\]

Solution 9:
The SDE  

\[
dW^{\mathbb P}_t = dW^{\mathbb Q^{(\lambda)}}_t-\lambda\,W^{\mathbb P}_t\,dt ,\qquad t\ge 0,
\]

is a linear stochastic differential equation of the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck type.  
Let  

\[
X_t:=W^{\mathbb P}_t ,\qquad B_t:=W^{\mathbb Q^{(\lambda)}}_t .
\]

Hence  

\[
dX_t = dB_t-\lambda X_t\,dt .
\]

---

### 1.  Integrating factor

Multiply both sides by the deterministic factor \(e^{\lambda t}\):

\[
e^{\lambda t} dX_t = e^{\lambda t} dB_t-\lambda e^{\lambda t} X_t dt .
\]

Now use the product rule for Itô calculus:

\[
d\bigl(e^{\lambda t} X_t\bigr)=e^{\lambda t} dX_t+\lambda e^{\lambda t} X_t dt .
\]

Substituting the expression for \(e^{\lambda t} dX_t\) we obtain the cancellation of the drift term:

\[
d\bigl(e^{\lambda t} X_t\bigr)=e^{\lambda t} dB_t .
\]

---

### 2.  Integrate from \(0\) to \(t\)

Integrating the last equality gives

\[
e^{\lambda t} X_t- e^{\lambda\cdot0} X_0 = \int_{0}^{t} e^{\lambda s}\, dB_s .
\]

Assuming the Brownian motions start at zero (\(X_0 = B_0=0\)), we have

\[
e^{\lambda t} X_t = \int_{0}^{t} e^{\lambda s}\, dB_s .
\]

---

### 3.  Solve for \(X_t\)

\[
X_t = e^{-\lambda t}\int_{0}^{t} e^{\lambda s}\, dB_s .
\]

Returning to the original notation \(X_t=W^{\mathbb P}_t\) and \(B_t=W^{\mathbb Q^{(\lambda)}}_t\),

\[
\boxed{\,W^{\mathbb P}_t = e^{-\lambda t}\int_{0}^{t} e^{\lambda s}\, dW^{\mathbb Q^{(\lambda)}}_s\, }.
\]

---

### 4.  Remarks  

* The integral on the right‑hand side is an Itô integral; it is a Gaussian random variable with mean \(0\) and variance  

  \[
  \operatorname{Var}\!\left(W^{\mathbb P}_t\right)
  =e^{-2\lambda t}\int_{0}^{t} e^{2\lambda s}\,ds
  =\frac{1-e^{-2\lambda t}}{2\lambda}\quad(\lambda\neq 0),
  \]

  which is the familiar variance of an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process.

* If \(\lambda =0\) the formula reduces to the trivial identity \(W^{\mathbb P}_t=W^{\mathbb Q^{(0)}}_t\).

Thus the solution of the SDE expressed explicitly in terms of the Brownian motion under the measure \(\mathbb{Q}^{(\lambda)}\) is given above.

Solution 10:
**Step 1 – Write the SDE in the linear form**

\[
dW^{\mathbb P}_t =-\,\lambda W^{\mathbb P}_t\,dt + dW^{\mathbb Q^{(\lambda)}}_t,
\qquad t\ge 0 .
\]

It is a linear Itô SDE with drift coefficient \(-\lambda\) and diffusion coefficient \(1\).

---

**Step 2 – Apply the integrating‑factor method**

Set  

\[
Y_t:=e^{\lambda t}W^{\mathbb P}_t .
\]

Because \(e^{\lambda t}\) is deterministic, Itô’s product rule gives  

\[
dY_t = e^{\lambda t}\,dW^{\mathbb P}_t +\lambda e^{\lambda t}W^{\mathbb P}_t\,dt
      = e^{\lambda t}\bigl(-\lambda W^{\mathbb P}_t\,dt + dW^{\mathbb Q^{(\lambda)}}_t\bigr)
        +\lambda e^{\lambda t}W^{\mathbb P}_t\,dt
      = e^{\lambda t} dW^{\mathbb Q^{(\lambda)}}_t .
\]

Thus  

\[
Y_t = Y_0 +\int_{0}^{t} e^{\lambda s}\,dW^{\mathbb Q^{(\lambda)}}_s .
\]

---

**Step 3 – Express \(W^{\mathbb P}_t\)**  

Since \(Y_t=e^{\lambda t}W^{\mathbb P}_t\),

\[
W^{\mathbb P}_t = e^{-\lambda t}\Bigl( Y_0
   + \int_{0}^{t} e^{\lambda s}\,dW^{\mathbb Q^{(\lambda)}}_s\Bigr).
\]

If the Brownian motions start at \(0\) (as usual), \(W^{\mathbb P}_0=0\) and \(Y_0=0\), whence

\[
\boxed{\,W^{\mathbb P}_t
      = e^{-\lambda t}\int_{0}^{t} e^{\lambda s}\,dW^{\mathbb Q^{(\lambda)}}_s
      = \int_{0}^{t} e^{-\lambda (t-s)}\,dW^{\mathbb Q^{(\lambda)}}_s\, }.
\]

More generally, with an arbitrary initial value \(W^{\mathbb P}_0=w_0\),

\[
\boxed{\,W^{\mathbb P}_t
      = w_0\,e^{-\lambda t}
        + \int_{0}^{t} e^{-\lambda (t-s)}\,dW^{\mathbb Q^{(\lambda)}}_s\, } .
\]

This formula gives the explicit representation of the \(\mathbb{P}\)-Brownian motion in terms of the \(\mathbb{Q}^{(\lambda)}\)-Brownian motion.
